title: qt: Workaround gcc 12.1 optimization bug with Qt
description:
The Qt implicit casts from QByteArray to QString all use
size = -1, meaning to the end of the string.

This causes gcc 12.1 with -O2 to produce a very dubious stringop-overread
warning, by computing both sides of a branch even when it shouldn't:

/usr/include/qt5/QtCore/qstring.h:706:69: error: ‘size_t strlen(const char*)’ reading 1 or more bytes from a region of size 0 [-Werror=stringop-overread]
  706 |         return fromUtf8_helper(str, (str && size == -1) ? int(strlen(str)) : size);
      |                                                               ~~~~~~^~~~~

There's also a similar error with QByteArray.constData(), even though
isEmpty() should return True when the QByteArray is NULL.
(Adding isNull() prevents the warning but is redundant.)

Use #pragma to ignore the warning on GCC, restoring settings afterward.
Fix #18090.

notes.body: assigned to @johnthacker
assigned to @jvalverde
I don't love this workaround, but it does work, especially since `qstrlen` is a safe call that returns 0 even when passed NULL). If anyone has any better ideas, feel free.

I hate this workaround as well. Especially because it seems to contradict Qt by not using the method as it would be possible. We can’t be the only ones with this issue, can we? Might be worth checking out other options

Perhaps just turning off the warning with a `#pragma GCC diagnostic ignored "-Wstringop-overread"` and then turning it back on after the statements until it gets fixed upstream is the better way to go?
This is usually done using the DIAG_OFF/DIAG_ON macros instead (in ws_diag_control.h).

Ah, thanks. That would help to avoid warnings that become errors for unknown pragmas.

Worst case, CMakeLists.txt can add -Wno-error=stringop-overrun for gcc 12.1, but it seems like overkill

So this should work. I've tested the about dialog and a few different files for Show Packet Bytes and Follow, and it works fine. As expected, because those code paths should never be followed and the warning is spurious.

How about folding the version check into the DIAG macros like is done elsewhere? Something like:

```
  #if WS_IS_AT_LEAST_GNUC_VERSION(12,1)
    #define DIAG_OFF_STRINGOP_OVERREAD DIAG_OFF(stringop-overread)
    #define DIAG_ON_STRINGOP_OVERREAD DIAG_ON(stringop-overread)
  #else
    #define DIAG_OFF_STRINGOP_OVERREAD
    #define DIAG_ON_STRINGOP_OVERREAD
  #endif
```

Hmm, I'm not sure. [gcc 11.1](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-11.1.0/gcc/Warning-Options.html#Warning-Options) is where the `stringop-overread` warning was introduced (enabled by default), it just does not have false positives triggered by the Qt code. If the version check were folded into the macro, should it include version 11.1 and greater?

For these specific lines, it doesn't need to be disabled for 11.1 (and arguably shouldn't therefore), but a generic DIAG macro should presumably disable it for all the versions of GCC for which the warning exists.
[gcc-10.3](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-10.3.0/gcc/Warning-Options.html#Warning-Options) does not have `stringop-overread` (only `stringop-overflow` and `stringop-truncation`).

The offending line of code appears to be

    yaml_text += "      " + base64_data.toBase64() + "\n";

The complaint appears to be that, somewhere, `QStrings::fromUtf8()` is getting passed, as the first argument, a pointer to the first element of a possibly zero-length array of bytes (even though such a thing can't really exist in C++, as far as I can tell - no zero-length arrays), and, as the second argument, -1, so that it has to determine the length of the string by scanning for a terminating `'\0'`, which won't work if there are *no* characters to scan.

What version of Qt is on the machine on which the build is being done?  In 5.12.12, in qbytearray.h, we have

```
inline const QByteArray operator+(const char *a1, const QByteArray &a2)
{ return QByteArray(a1) += a2; }
```

which is presumably the `+` operator in `"      " + base64_data.toBase64()`.  The next `+` would presumably be

```
inline const QByteArray operator+(const QByteArray &a1, const char *a2)
{ return QByteArray(a1) += a2; }
```

Presumably the idea is that `QByteArray(a1)` creates a new `QByteArray`, so you don't append to the one passed as the first argument, and that the second argument is used to construct another `QByteArray` appended to the first one.

Concatenating three `QByteArray`s, at least two of which are not null, shouldn't ever produce a null `QByteArray`, so this *shoul* be safe.

I guess G++ doesn't understand that, and is quaking in terror at the thought that  in

```
    inline QT_ASCII_CAST_WARN QString &operator+=(const QByteArray &s)
    { return append(QString::fromUtf8(s)); }
```

from qstring.h, `s` might be an empty `QByteArray`.  However, we also have

```
    static inline QString fromUtf8(const QByteArray &str)
    { return str.isNull() ? QString() : fromUtf8(str.data(), qstrnlen(str.constData(), str.size())); }
```

which should protect against that.

Or is some weird C++ rule getting in the way of making sure that we always choose the right method and safely handle zero-length `QByteArray`s?  I don't see why there should *be* any implicit casts from `QByteArray` to `QString`; I'm not seeing any `QString`s on the RHS of the `+=`, nor am I seeing any in the `+=` operator itself.

> I don't see why there should be any implicit casts from QByteArray to QString; I'm not seeing any QStrings on the RHS of the +=, nor am I seeing any in the += operator itself.

There's a cast to QString because the LHS, `yaml_text` in that instance (and similarly in the other places) is a QString.

The version of Qt is 5.15.3, but the code in qstring.h is the same, including eventually calling this:
```c++
    static inline QString fromUtf8(const char *str, int size = -1)
    {
        return fromUtf8_helper(str, (str && size == -1) ? int(strlen(str)) : size);
    }
```

Either way, the checks to see if str is null (either as a `const char *` or as a `QByteArray`) should eliminate the problem even if one of the `QByteArray`s could be null which, as you note, it cannot because we're constructing it so at minimum it is a empty null terminated string. One of our checks even checks `isEmpty` and it still produces the warning.

All I can assume is that the optimizer in the compiler is for some reason assuming that it might, for speed or branch prediction or something, calculate `strlen(str)` before determining that `str` is null.

> The complaint appears to be that, somewhere, `QStrings::fromUtf8()` is getting passed, as the first argument, a pointer to the first element of a possibly zero-length array of bytes (even though such a thing can't really exist in C++, as far as I can tell - no zero-length arrays),

And even though you could, in C. manage to make such a thing happen, the compiler should either keep its mouth shut unless it knows for certain that the byte array is zero-length or should say something such as "size_t strlen(const char\*)’ *possibly* reading 1 or more bytes from a region of size 0 [-Werror=stringop-overread]".

@@ -950,7 +950,17 @@ void WiresharkMainWindow::startCapture(QStringList interfaces _U_) {
                     /* Not the first selected interface; is its capture filter
                        the same as the one the other interfaces we've looked
                        at have? */
+                    /* XXX: GCC 12.1 has a bogus warning at -O2 and higher
+                     * even though the isEmpty() check guarantees that
+                     * filter_ba.constData() is never NULL or empty.
+                     */
+#if WS_IS_AT_LEAST_GNUC_VERSION(12,1)
+DIAG_OFF(stringop-overread)
+#endif
                     if (strcmp(interface_opts->cfilter, filter_ba.constData()) != 0) {
+#if WS_IS_AT_LEAST_GNUC_VERSION(12,1)
+DIAG_ON(stringop-overread)
+#endif
                         /* No, so not all selected interfaces have the same capture
                            filter. */
                         filter_ba.clear();
